info.title: Worker Management API
info.description: Multi-tenant API for creating LLM-powered workers, sending messages to agents, tracking worker state, and executing DAG workflow graphs. Supports five agent types (pydantic-ai, claude-code, codex, remote-claude, remote-codex) and six model providers (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Groq, Cohere, MLX, inference-router). Workers produce structured output validated against JSON Schema. All data is tenant-isolated via license-token authentication.

get.description:
Get all worker state records across all workers for a specific tenant.

Retrieves all state records from all workers for the specified tenant. This is useful
for system-wide monitoring, debugging, or analytics. Use with caution in
production as it may return a large amount of data.

Args:
    tenant_id: Tenant identifier for multi-tenancy

Returns:
    Dict containing:
        - states: List of all state records from all workers
        - total: Total number of state records returned

Raises:
    HTTPException: 500 if database query fails

Note:
    No pagination is currently implemented. For large deployments,
    consider using per-worker state queries instead.

Examples:
    Response:
    ```json
    {
        "states": [
            {
                "id": 1,
                "worker_id": "123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000",
                "worker_name": "data_processor",
                "state_type": "completed",
                "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
                "worker_state": {"status": "completed"}
            },
            ...
        ],
        "total": 150
    }
    ```

delete.description:
Delete all worker state records for a specific tenant while leaving workers intact.

Removes all historical state data from all workers for the specified tenant. This is
a destructive operation that cannot be undone. The workers themselves remain
registered and functional - only their state history is cleared.

Args:
    tenant_id: Tenant identifier for multi-tenancy

Use cases:
- Clearing old data to free up database space
- Resetting the system for testing
- Compliance with data retention policies

Returns:
    None (204 No Content on success)

Raises:
    HTTPException: 500 if database operation fails

Warning:
    This operation is irreversible. All state history for this tenant will be permanently lost.

Note:
    Returns 204 No Content on successful deletion. The number of deleted
    records is logged but not returned to the client.

get.description:
Get state history for a specific worker for a specific tenant.

Retrieves the historical state records for a worker, ordered by timestamp
(most recent first). This is useful for debugging, monitoring worker activity,
and understanding the worker's processing history.

Args:
    worker_name: Name of the worker to get state history for
    limit: Maximum number of state records to return (1-100, default 10)
    tenant_id: Tenant identifier for multi-tenancy

Returns:
    List of state records, each containing:
        - id: State record ID
        - worker_id: Worker's unique ID
        - worker_name: Worker's name
        - is_agent: Whether worker is an agent
        - state_type: Type of state (created, processing, completed, error)
        - timestamp: When the state was recorded
        - metadata: Optional metadata
        - worker_state: The actual state data

Raises:
    HTTPException: 422 if worker name is invalid
    HTTPException: 404 if worker not found
    HTTPException: 500 if database query fails

Examples:
    GET /workers/data_processor/states?limit=5

    Returns last 5 state records for the data_processor worker

get.description:
Get the most recent state for a worker for a specific tenant.

Retrieves only the latest state record for a worker. This is useful for
checking the current status or the result of the most recent operation.

Args:
    worker_name: Name of the worker to get latest state for
    tenant_id: Tenant identifier for multi-tenancy

Returns:
    Dict containing the latest state record with:
        - id: State record ID
        - worker_id: Worker's unique ID
        - worker_name: Worker's name
        - is_agent: Whether worker is an agent
        - state_type: Type of state (created, processing, completed, error)
        - timestamp: When the state was recorded
        - metadata: Optional metadata
        - worker_state: The actual state data including status and any results

Raises:
    HTTPException: 404 if worker not found or no state exists
    HTTPException: 500 if database query fails

Examples:
    Response for a completed task:
    ```json
    {
        "id": 42,
        "worker_id": "123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000",
        "worker_name": "data_processor",
        "is_agent": true,
        "state_type": "completed",
        "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
        "worker_state": {
            "status": "completed",
            "message": "Process the dataset",
            "response": "Dataset processed successfully. 1000 records analyzed."
        }
    }
    ```

delete.description:
Force cleanup of a worker instance from the cache.

This endpoint forcefully removes a worker instance from the in-memory cache
without deleting the worker registration. This is useful for:
- Clearing stuck or unhealthy worker instances
- Forcing recreation of a worker on next use
- Freeing memory from unused worker instances

The worker registration remains intact, so the worker can be recreated
automatically on the next request.

Args:
    worker_name: Name of the worker instance to cleanup.
                Must be valid Unicode identifier (no control chars, commas, or whitespace)

Returns:
    Dict containing:
        - status: Confirmation message "Worker instance cleaned up"

Raises:
    HTTPException: 422 if worker name is invalid (empty, reserved word,
                  invalid characters, too long)
    HTTPException: 500 if cleanup fails

Note:
    This operation only affects the cached instance, not the worker registration.
    Reserved names like 'null', 'undefined', 'true', 'false' are rejected.
    Maximum length is 200 bytes when UTF-8 encoded.

Examples:
    DELETE /workers/data_processor/instance

    Response:
    ```json
    {
        "status": "Worker instance cleaned up"
    }
    ```

delete.description:
Delete a specific worker and all associated states for a specific tenant.

Completely removes a worker from the system including:
1. All state history records
2. Worker instance from cache (with cleanup)
3. Worker registration from database

This operation is irreversible. The worker would need to be recreated
to use it again.

Args:
    worker_name: Name of the worker to delete.
                Must be 1-100 characters.
    tenant_id: Tenant identifier for multi-tenancy

Returns:
    None (204 No Content on success)

Raises:
    HTTPException: 422 if worker name is empty
    HTTPException: 404 if worker not found
    HTTPException: 500 if deletion fails

Note:
    The operation is designed to be resilient - it will attempt to clean up
    all resources even if some steps fail. For example, if state deletion
    fails, it will still proceed with worker removal.

parameters.name: worker_name

schema.description: Name of the worker to delete
schema.title: Worker Name

parameters.description: Name of the worker to delete

delete.description:
Delete all workers and their associated states for a specific tenant.

Completely removes all workers for the specified tenant including:
1. All state history records for all workers
2. All worker instances from cache (with cleanup)
3. All worker registrations from database

This operation is scoped to the (tenant_id, subject_id) and does not affect other tenants' or other users' workers.
This operation is irreversible. All workers would need to be recreated
to use them again.

Args:
    tenant_id: Tenant identifier for multi-tenancy

Returns:
    None (204 No Content on success)

Raises:
    HTTPException: 500 if deletion fails

Use cases:
- Clearing all workers to reset the system for testing
- System maintenance or cleanup
- Starting fresh with a clean slate

Warning:
    This operation is irreversible. All workers and their state history
    for this tenant will be permanently lost.

Note:
    The operation is designed to be resilient - it will attempt to clean up
    all resources even if some steps fail. For example, if state deletion
    fails for some workers, it will still proceed with worker removal.

get.description:
Retrieve worker states from the database with pagination for a specific tenant.

Fetches worker state records from the state database with pagination support.
This endpoint returns the state history for all workers belonging to the specified tenant.

Args:
    tenant_id: Tenant identifier for multi-tenancy
    limit: Maximum number of worker states to return (1-1000, default: 100)
    offset: Number of worker states to skip for pagination (default: 0)

Returns:
    List of dictionaries, each containing:
        - id: State record ID
        - worker_id: Unique worker identifier
        - worker_name: Human-readable worker name
        - is_agent: Whether the worker is an AI agent
        - state_type: Type of state (created, processing, completed, error, etc.)
        - timestamp: When the state was recorded (ISO format)
        - metadata: Optional metadata dictionary
        - worker_state: The actual state data dictionary

Raises:
    HTTPException: 500 with detailed error message for:
        - Database connection/operational errors
        - File system errors
        - Runtime errors
        - Unexpected errors

Examples:

    ```json
    [
        {
            "id": 1,
            "worker_id": "worker_123",
            "worker_name": "data_processor",
            "is_agent": true,
            "state_type": "completed",
            "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
            "metadata": {"task_id": "task_456"},
            "worker_state": {
    ```

post.description:
Save multiple worker states to the database for a specific tenant.

Batch endpoint for saving worker states. Accepts up to 100 state records
in a single request. Each state is validated and saved individually.
Extra fields not defined in the schema are rejected with 422 errors.

Args:
    tenant_id: Tenant identifier for multi-tenancy
    worker_states: List of SaveWorkerStateRequest objects (max 100), each containing:
        - worker_id: Unique worker identifier (1-100 chars)
        - worker_name: Human-readable worker name (1-100 chars)
        - state_type: Valid state type enum value
        - timestamp: Optional timestamp (defaults to current time)
        - worker_state: Required state data dictionary (max 50KB)

Returns:
    Dict containing:
        - message: Success confirmation message
        - results: List of saved state records with:
            - id: Generated state record ID
            - worker_id: Worker identifier

Raises:
    HTTPException: 422 for validation errors:
        - Empty or null worker_id/worker_name
        - Invalid state_type value
        - Missing or non-dict worker_state
        - Extra fields in request body
        - worker_state larger than 50KB
    HTTPException: 500 for server errors:
        - Database connection/operational errors
        - File system errors
        - Runtime errors
        - Unexpected errors

Note:
    - is_agent defaults to False as it's not in the request model
    - metadata is set to None as it's not in the request model
    - Each state is saved individually (not transactional)
    - Timestamp defaults to current time if not provided

Examples:
    Request:
    ```json
    {
        "worker_states": [
            {
                "worker_id": "worker_123",
                "worker_name": "data_processor",
                "state_type": "processing",
                "worker_state": {
                    "current_operation": "analyzing_data",
                    "processed_records": 1500
                }
            }
        ]
    }
    ```

    Response:
    ```json
    {
        "message": "Workers' states saved successfully",
        "results": [
            {
                "id": 42,
                "worker_id": "worker_123"
            }
        ]
    }
    ```

get.description:
List execution sessions visible under (tenant_id, subject_id) with filters.

Each row carries the persisted session columns including ``session_id``,
``request_payload``, ``final_response``, ``correlation_id``,
``validation_passed``, ``status``, ``created_at``, and ``completed_at``.
``request_payload`` / ``final_response`` are the input/output shapes the
eval-set sampler needs to redact and persist as ``eval_tuples``; the
model-evaluator side maps them through the existing redact + insert path
(``POST /eval-sets/{id}/refresh-from-prod``). ``session_id`` and
``correlation_id`` are persisted onto the eval_tuple as provenance.

Filters compose with AND. ``since`` / ``until`` bracket ``created_at``
(closed lower bound, open upper bound). UUIDs are validated when supplied.

Visibility: returns tenant-visible rows the caller would see directly. With
no ``X-Subject-Id`` forwarded, ``visibility='user'`` rows belonging to
other subjects are excluded by design — refresh-from-wm cannot reach
user-private traces.

get.description:
Return all sessions tagged with ``correlation_id`` under the caller's scope.

Used by the metering_service ``exec_quality`` ETL to enrich the three
columns currently left NULL (``validation_passed``, ``quality_score``,
``retry_count``). Returns ``[]`` → HTTP 404 so the ETL can branch on
a single status code; 200 with an empty list would force the ETL to
inspect the body to disambiguate "not yet" from "service error".

Visibility (two paths):

* **In-tenant callers** (default): tenant_id-restricted; user-private
  rows belonging to other subjects are filtered out. Cross-tenant
  requests for an existing correlation_id return 404 (not 403) to
  avoid leaking existence per the service-isolation invariant.

* **Internal-service callers** (caller in ``_INTERNAL_SERVICE_ROLES``,
  e.g. metering-internal): scope filter is bypassed; the row is
  returned regardless of which tenant owns it. Every cross-tenant
  read is audit-logged with caller client_id + observed tenant_id.

404 when no row exists for ``(card_type, list)`` OR when the row has no
prior version to roll back to. Both are caller errors and the caller
must not blindly retry.

On success, fires the ``workflowAutoRollback`` webhook to fr-backend
(best-effort; swallowed failures).

ImageBlock.title: ImageBlock
ImageBlock.description:
Image content block for multimodal messages.

``data`` is the base64-encoded image bytes. ``media_type`` is the
MIME type (image/jpeg, image/png, image/webp, image/gif).
Decoded payload is capped at ~10 MB per image to prevent OOM
on the worker pod.

trust_content.title: Trust Content
trust_content.description: Skip command-injection pattern detection on message + prompt fields. For trusted callers submitting document-as-text content (markdown with code snippets, scraped pages with shell examples, LLM ingestion pipelines) where curl/bash/$(...)/&& are content, not adversarial. All other security checks (null bytes, control chars, length cap, SQL/XSS/path-traversal/LDAP) remain active. License-authz is the trust boundary that gates who can set this.

message.title: Message
message.description: Message to send to the agent. Either a plain string (~1M tokens at 5 chars/token, max 5M chars) or a list of typed content blocks for multimodal input (text + image). Multimodal lists are only supported by agent_type='pydantic_ai' workers configured against a vision-capable model (claude-sonnet-4-5, gpt-4o, gemini-2-pro, gemma-4).

MessageRequest.title: MessageRequest
MessageRequest.description:
Request model for sending messages to agents.

This model supports both sending messages to existing workers and creating
new workers on-the-fly. If a worker doesn't exist, it will be automatically
created with default settings (temperature=0.1, model=deepseek-chat).

The output_schema and output_validator fields allow per-message structured
output configuration, overriding the worker's default schema for this specific
message.

examples.message: Analyze the sales data from Q4 2023 and identify the top performing products
examples.system_prompt: You are a data analyst specializing in sales performance metrics

When creating edges, ensure they reference the actual node IDs from
the nodes list, not hardcoded example UUIDs.
